meta.subtitle: Fiscal Q3 revenue rose 40% and adjusted operating margin reached 50.0%, but at 25.7x FY27E consensus EPS the upswing is largely in the price

analystCommentary:
ADI's fiscal third quarter 2026, ended August 1, 2026, improved on revenue, margins, cash flow and outlook alike. For a buyer at $420.83, the question is how much of the next year the price already carries, not whether the upswing is real.

In our reading, most of it. The valuation section shows the stock priced on fiscal 2027 consensus earnings, and the financials and risk sections show margins at a level the last downturn did not hold. Those two facts together cap the upside we can underwrite.

The franchise and the near-term momentum keep us from SELL. The company has guided the fourth quarter higher, nothing in the current data shows the cycle turning, and the moat section explains why we expect cash generation to hold up better than earnings if it does.

Weighting the scenarios leaves modest expected upside against a meaningful Bear downside. That is too little reward to add at this price and too little risk to sell. We rate ADI HOLD.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
Analog Devices, Inc. designs, manufactures, tests and markets integrated circuits, software and subsystems. Its products include data converters, power management and reference products, power ICs, amplifiers, radio frequency and microwave ICs, micro-electro-mechanical systems such as accelerometers, gyroscopes and inertial measurement units, isolators, and digital signal processing and system products. It serves industrial, automotive, consumer, instrumentation, aerospace, defense and healthcare, and communications customers through a direct sales force, third-party distributors, independent sales representatives and online. The company was incorporated in 1965 and is headquartered in Wilmington, Massachusetts.

ADI reports as a single segment. Fiscal 2025, which ended November 1, 2025, brought revenue of $11.0B, and the 10-Q under review covers the fiscal third quarter 2026, ended August 1, 2026. At $420.83 a share the market values the company at about $203.9B.

We see a broad, high-margin supplier of analog, mixed-signal and power chips whose earnings still rise and fall with the semiconductor cycle. That cycle, more than the quality of the franchise, is what decides the call.

thesis.body:
HOLD, target range $430–$470. ADI is in a broad upswing: fiscal third-quarter revenue rose 40% year over year, adjusted operating margin reached 50.0%, and the company guided the fourth quarter higher again.

The price already leans on the next leg. At 25.7x FY27E consensus EPS of $16.35, the stock needs fiscal 2027 to deliver another year of growth, and a cyclical turn would take earnings and the multiple down together. Weighting our three scenarios gives modest expected upside against a Bear downside large enough to keep reward/risk well short of the BUY bar.

catalysts: Fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 results against the August 19, 2026 outlook of $4.3 billion in revenue, plus or minus $100 million.
Further growth in the data center sub-market, which the company says led growth within Communications.
Evidence that fiscal 2027 revenue and EPS can meet or beat the consensus the thesis relies on.
Continued cash returns, led by the $1.10 quarterly dividend declared with the third-quarter results.
risks: A cyclical turn from margins that already sit above every fiscal year in the table.
A de-rating from near the top of the 52-week range if FY27E estimates slip.
Export restrictions and trade policy affecting China, which the fiscal 2025 10-K says have already affected revenue.
Reliance on distributors, which carried 58% of third-quarter revenue.

financials.incomeCommentary:
Fiscal third-quarter 2026 revenue was $4.02 billion, {+ up 40% +} year over year, and nine-month revenue rose 36%. The company attributes the increase to "broad-based demand across end markets"; the growth section covers the end-market detail.

Gross margin rose to 67.3% from 62.1%, a gain of 520 basis points that ADI attributes "primarily" to "higher utilization of our manufacturing fixed costs as a result of increased customer demand and favorable mix of products sold into our end markets." Operating margin reached 40.1% against 28.4% a year earlier. R&D expenses rose 17% and SMG&A expenses 22%, yet they fell to 13% and 10% of revenue from 16% and 11%, which the company credits to "higher revenue levels and improved operating leverage."

Reported EPS growth overstates the underlying gain. Diluted EPS rose 163% to $2.74 from $1.04, but the year-ago quarter carried a $153.8 million net deferred tax expense tied to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which lifted its effective tax rate to 32.1% against 13.3% this quarter. This quarter's special charges line also includes a $24.4 million gain on the sale of a subsidiary in Penang, Malaysia. Adjusted diluted EPS, which excludes acquisition-related expenses, acquisition-related transaction costs and special charges, net, rose 68% to $3.45 from $2.05, and adjusted operating margin reached 50.0% from 42.2%. We treat the adjusted growth rate as the better guide to the trend.

Profitability is now above anything in the five-year table. The trailing operating margin of 35.5% compares with no more than 31.1% (FY23) in any fiscal year shown. We read that as a cyclically high level rather than a new floor; the risk section sets out what the last downturn did to margins.
financials.balanceCommentary:
The latest full balance sheet in the tables is fiscal 2025's, at November 1, 2025: total debt of $8.6B, cash and short-term investments of $3.7B, net debt of $6.1B and total equity of $33.8B. The 10-Q adds that cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments were $2.3 billion at August 1, 2026, approximately $1.0 billion of it held in the United States. The excerpt gives no updated debt figure, so we do not restate net debt for the quarter.

Leverage is modest against current earnings, with trailing net debt/EBITDA of 1.0x and interest coverage of 14.1x. Those ratios are measured on upswing EBITDA, though. Against FY24 EBITDA of $4.1B, the fiscal 2025 debt load would look noticeably heavier, which is the relevant test if the cycle turns.

Liquidity has tightened since year-end. The trailing current ratio of 1.25 compares with 2.19 at fiscal 2025 year-end, and the reason is not given. ADI says it believes its liquidity, cash from operations and "existing and anticipated available short- and long-term financing" will be sufficient "for at least the next twelve months." We agree that the balance sheet is no constraint today, but it carries less cushion than it did at year-end.
financials.cashflowCommentary:
Cash generation is a clear strength. The release reports trailing-twelve-month operating cash flow of $5.5 billion and free cash flow of $4.9 billion, and it puts that free cash flow at a higher share of revenue than the 29.8% trailing net margin, so cash earnings exceed reported earnings.

Conversion slipped over the nine months. Operating cash flow was 36% of revenue against 39% a year earlier, even as net income rose 126%. ADI attributes the higher operating cash flow to "higher net income adjusted for non-cash items", which leaves the lower ratio unexplained. We treat it as something to track rather than a warning.

Capital spending is light. FY25 capital expenditure was $533.6M, against $1.3B in FY23, so nearly all operating cash reaches free cash flow. How that cash is being returned, and whether returns now outrun it, is covered under capital allocation.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
The shares trade at $420.83, near the top of a 52-week range of $223.47–$445.91. That is a sharp move off the low within a year. None of the filings or releases we draw on explains it, and we do not assign it a cause, but it means the starting multiple already reflects a strong run.

The headline multiples sit on different earnings bases. The trailing P/E of 49.9x rests on reported diluted EPS. The vendor labels 32.6x a forward (NTM) P/E, but it lines up with the current price over FY26E consensus EPS of $12.89, so it is in effect a multiple on the fiscal year now closing. The ~25.7x is on FY27E consensus EPS of $16.35. Both consensus EPS figures appear to be on the company's adjusted basis: nine-month reported diluted EPS of $6.83 plus the fourth-quarter reported EPS outlook of $3.14 falls well short of the FY26E figure. The step down from the trailing multiple to the FY27E multiple therefore mixes a change of earnings basis with expected growth, and only part of it is growth.

Trailing EV/EBITDA is 30.5x and the trailing free-cash-flow yield is 2.4%, against a dividend yield of 1.05%. No peer multiples are available, so we judge these against ADI's own earnings path. On that path, a cash yield that low leaves little cushion if fiscal 2027 falls short.

The Street is firmly positive: 30 of 34 analysts rate the stock Buy, 4 Hold and none Sell. The consensus target of $470.72 implies +11.9%, the median is $463.50, and targets run from $365.00 to $675.00, so the high end lifts the mean. We anchor our Base case to the median, and we note that even the Street's central case leaves only moderate upside from here.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Basis: 32.6x, today's multiple on current-year (FY26E) consensus EPS, applied to FY27E consensus EPS of $16.35. Fiscal 2027 delivers consensus and, a year from now, the market still pays that current-year multiple. That needs demand to keep strengthening into fiscal 2028 and adjusted margins to hold near the fourth-quarter outlook.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Basis: the median Street target of $463.50, which values FY27E consensus EPS at a multiple between today's FY27E multiple and the current-year multiple used in the Bull case. Fiscal 2027 delivers consensus, growth slows from the fiscal 2026 pace as consensus already expects, and the cycle does not turn within the year.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Basis: 25.7x, today's FY27E multiple, applied to FY26E consensus EPS of $12.89. The cycle turns during fiscal 2027, as it did in FY24: earnings stall near the fiscal 2026 level instead of reaching FY27E consensus, and the market pays the lower forward multiple rather than the current-year one. The result sits below the lowest Street target of $365.00.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
All three scenarios value ADI on fiscal 2027 earnings using multiples and EPS figures a reader can check above. They differ on two things: whether FY27E consensus EPS arrives, and what multiple the market pays for it.

The Base case carries 50% because the near-term evidence supports consensus. The company guided fourth-quarter revenue sequentially higher, and as the growth section shows, FY26E consensus revenue matches that outlook, so the Street is not ahead of the company on fiscal 2026.

The Bull case carries 25%. It needs the market to keep paying today's current-year multiple on a larger earnings base a year from now, which in turn needs the growth story to extend into fiscal 2028. Nothing in the outlook reaches that far.

The Bear case carries the same weight as the Bull, argued on the Bear itself. The revenue table shows one down year in five, FY24, and it came after a year of little growth; ADI is now in its second year of growth with margins at the cyclical high described under Financials, the point in the cycle where a turn costs most. Against that, the CFO's comment on strengthening demand and the higher fourth-quarter outlook show no turn yet, so we do not weight it above a quarter. A full repeat of FY24, with earnings falling well below the FY26E level and the shares revisiting their 52-week low, is a tail outside these scenarios rather than a reason to raise the Bear weight.

The weighted result is expected upside of +6.4% against a Bear-case downside of -21.3%, a reward/risk of 0.30×, which derives HOLD. The call is not close. Moving ten points of weight from Base to Bull leaves expected upside short of the BUY line, and moving ten points to Bear leaves it positive. A BUY would need a Bull weight well above the Base weight, which the evidence does not support.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: ADI reports one segment, and its 10-Q splits revenue by end market and by channel. In the fiscal third quarter 2026, Industrial was 49% of revenue (45% a year earlier), Automotive 25% (30%), Communications 16% (12%) and Consumer 10% (13%), so the mix is shifting toward the two end markets that grew faster than the company total. Distributors, which buy products with the intention of reselling them, carried 58% of revenue against 55% a year earlier, and direct customers, mainly original equipment manufacturers, 39% against 43%. ADI says the distributor share rose "primarily due to the increase in the percentage of revenue from our Industrial end market." The 2026 proxy statement puts "Business-to-Business Revenue" at ~87% for fiscal 2025. The shift makes ADI more geared to industrial demand and data center spending than a year ago, which adds growth in an upswing and exposure in a downturn. It also leaves more than half of revenue reflecting distributor purchases rather than direct end demand, a point the risk section takes up.

moatFactors.name: Cash margins through the cycle
moatFactors.body: Across FY21–FY25, gross margin never fell below 57.1%, its FY24 level in the year revenue fell, and free-cash-flow margin never fell below 28.9% (FY23). FCF margin was 33.1% in the FY24 downturn itself. Holding cash margins at that level through a down year suggests pricing and cost advantages that are hard to copy. The advantage shows up in cash rather than in stable earnings.

moatFactors.name: Breadth and R&D commitment
moatFactors.body: ADI sells many product families into several end markets through several channels, so no single application carries the business. The 2026 proxy says ADI "invested a record amount to research and development in fiscal year 2025" to "further extend the technical and market leadership of our core analog, mixed signal, and power portfolio." Breadth backed by sustained R&D is the base of the franchise. The limit is that this evidence is the company's own description, and without peer data we cannot show the portfolio out-earns rivals.

moatFactors.name: Owned manufacturing
moatFactors.body: The CEO cites "manufacturing agility" as part of ADI's advantage, and the gross-margin gain described under Financials came from utilization of its own fixed manufacturing costs. Owning capacity lets ADI capture margin when demand is strong. It also leaves fixed costs that weigh on margins when demand falls, and the fiscal 2025 10-K lists significant operations and manufacturing outside the United States, including in Ireland, the Philippines, Thailand and Malaysia, which adds trade and geopolitical exposure.

moatFactors.name: Return on the capital base
moatFactors.body: Fiscal 2025 net income of $2.3B came on total equity of $33.8B, a modest return on the book the company carries even in a recovery year. Measured on free cash flow the return looks better, but this gap is why we stop short of WIDE: the evidence shows a franchise with durable cash margins, not one earning exceptional returns on the capital invested in it.

businessMoat.durability:
We rate the moat NARROW. Cash margins that held through FY24 and the breadth of the franchise argue for durability; the modest return on book equity keeps us from WIDE.

The main threat to durability is China. The fiscal 2025 10-K says export restrictions may cause customers to "replace our products with products from another supplier that is not subject to the export restrictions or focus on building indigenous semiconductor capacity to reduce reliance on U.S. suppliers." Competition is also a listed factor, as "our ability to compete successfully in the markets in which we operate."

Over a five-year view we expect the franchise to keep its cash margins in most markets, with the business tied to China the part most exposed to erosion.

points: Industrial, close to half of revenue, grew {+ 53% +} year over year in the fiscal third quarter 2026. The company says all Industrial sub-markets grew, "with test equipment and aerospace and defense representing the highest growth." Growth that broad in an end market of that size is the core of the upswing. Its counterweight is that Industrial also drove the higher distributor share of revenue, so part of this growth passed through the channel.

Communications grew {+ 84% +} year over year in the quarter and 72% over the nine months, ahead of the other three end markets. The company says "the strongest growth within Communications came from the data center sub-market, driven by artificial intelligence-related infrastructure investments." This is the main structural driver the company names, but Communications is still smaller than Industrial or Automotive and rests on one spending theme.

Automotive grew 16% and Consumer 6% in the quarter, both slower than the company as a whole. Automotive's quarterly rate beat its 9% nine-month rate, so it picked up in the third quarter, while Consumer's lagged its 18% nine-month rate, so it slowed. Consumer is the one end market where momentum is fading.

On August 19, 2026, ADI guided fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 revenue to $4.3 billion, plus or minus $100 million, above the third quarter even at the low end. It expects reported operating margin of approximately 42.6%, plus or minus 150 bps, and reported EPS of $3.14, plus or minus $0.15 (adjusted: approximately 52.0% and $3.86). The CFO called it a "record fourth quarter outlook", while the company notes actual results "may differ materially." The outlook supports the near term, not fiscal 2027.

Consensus expects FY26E revenue of $15.1B (+37%), in line with nine-month revenue plus the fourth-quarter outlook midpoint, and FY27E revenue of $18.2B with EPS of $16.35. Fiscal 2026 is largely set by the outlook; fiscal 2027 is where the debate sits, since it assumes a third straight year of growth. The release speaks to it through the CFO's aim to "carry that momentum into fiscal 2027," not with numbers.

management.leadership:
According to the 2026 proxy statement, Vincent Roche is Chief Executive Officer and Chair of the Board of Directors, and Richard C. Puccio, Jr. is Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer. The other named executive officers for fiscal 2025 were Martin Cotter (Senior Vice President, Vertical Business Units), Vivek Jain (Executive Vice President, Global Operations and Technology) and Katsu Nakamura (Senior Vice President and Chief Customer Officer).

In the August 19, 2026 release, Roche said ADI delivered results "exceeding the midpoint of our revenue, margin, and earnings outlook," and Puccio said "Demand continued to strengthen across our product portfolio and regions throughout the third quarter." We take the beat on the company's word. Roche's description of "a unique advantage to create, deliver, and capture value in the AI era" is forward-looking, and we do not score it.

The team is executing well in an upswing. The better test of management is its response when demand falls, and the FY24 cut to buybacks, covered under capital allocation, is the main evidence of that response.
management.capitalAllocation:
ADI returns most of its cash to shareholders. In fiscal 2025 it repurchased $2.2B of stock and paid $1.9B in dividends; the 2026 proxy reports more than $4 billion returned that year, more than $24B over ten years and a 10-year dividend CAGR of 9.5%. In the fiscal third quarter 2026 it returned $1.7 billion and declared a $1.10 quarterly dividend, payable September 15, 2026.

The pace now runs ahead of cash generation. The release's trailing-twelve-month cash-return table shows dividends and repurchases together exceeding free cash flow of $4.9 billion, while cash and short-term investments have fallen since fiscal year-end, as the balance-sheet discussion shows. ADI also recorded transaction costs in the quarter for the acquisition of Empower Semiconductor, Inc.

FY24 shows how management flexes. Repurchases fell to $0.6B from $3.0B in FY23, while dividends rose to $1.8B from $1.7B. Protecting the dividend and flexing the buyback is the right order for outside holders, and we expect it to repeat if the cycle turns, which makes buybacks, not the dividend, the lever at risk.
management.governance:
Governance evidence comes from the 2026 proxy statement, which covers fiscal 2025 pay and reports ownership as of January 8, 2026. Vincent Roche holds both the CEO and Chair roles. The excerpt does not show board independence or any lead director arrangement, so we cannot judge the counterweight to a combined CEO and Chair; on its face, the combination concentrates authority.

Pay design leans on performance. The proxy says "a significant portion of the total target compensation" for executive officers is "variable, performance-based incentive compensation," built from base salary, a variable cash incentive, time-based RSUs, relative TSR PRSUs and financial metric PRSUs; the excerpt cuts off before the target-mix figures. A relative TSR component ties part of pay to shareholder returns, which is the right alignment for outside holders.

The proxy reports no related person transactions requiring disclosure under Item 404 since the beginning of fiscal year 2025 through the proxy date, and a written policy under which the Audit Committee reviews related person transactions above $120,000. For outside holders the picture is clean on related parties and sensible on pay, with the combined CEO and Chair role as the one structural point against.
management.insiderOwnership:
No holder comes close to control. As of January 8, 2026, the proxy lists two holders of 5% or more: Vanguard Group Inc. with 49,618,676 shares beneficially owned, or 10.2%, and BlackRock Inc. with 38,733,607 shares, or 7.9%. Both rest on Schedule 13G amendments that report ownership as of February 28, 2025 for Vanguard and December 31, 2023 for BlackRock, so both figures are dated.

Insider stakes are small. All directors and executive officers as a group (15 persons) beneficially owned 1,771,101 shares, less than 1% of the stock. Vincent Roche's total beneficial ownership of 790,854 shares includes 686,226 shares acquirable within 60 days, so most of his position takes that form. No individual in the table reaches that threshold, including Ray Stata at 791,897 shares.

For outside holders, ADI is widely held, and insiders' alignment comes mainly through pay design rather than large personal stakes. That puts more weight on the board's oversight of capital allocation, where outside holders' interests are most directly at stake.

idiosyncratic: Operating leverage in reverse. The fixed-cost utilization that lifted gross margin this year works the other way when demand falls. FY24 shows the scale: revenue fell 23.4%, operating margin dropped to 21.6%, and diluted EPS fell to $3.28 from $6.55. With trailing margins now above FY23's, a downturn from here would start from a higher base and could cut earnings just as sharply. This is the main risk to the stock, and the Bear case prices a milder version of it.

China and export restrictions. The fiscal 2025 10-K says export restrictions "have impacted our revenues and results of operations in China and elsewhere" and that ADI expects they "may continue to have direct and indirect adverse impacts." Without a China revenue figure we cannot size the exposure. We treat it as an ongoing drag with a risk of escalation.

Distributor buying. With distributors carrying more than half of revenue, as described in the business section, reported revenue depends partly on distributor purchasing decisions. The 10-Q lists "performance of independent distributors" and the risk that "products may be diverted from our authorized distribution channels" among factors that could change results, and the 10-K names customers that "amass large inventories of our products" as one response to export restrictions. We cannot see channel inventory, so a correction would arrive with little notice.

Acquisition integration. ADI recorded transaction costs in the third quarter for the acquisition of Empower Semiconductor, Inc., and its price and timing are not stated in the documents we draw on. The 10-Q lists "unanticipated difficulties or expenditures relating to integrating acquired businesses" among its risk factors. Alongside the cash trends covered under capital allocation, a large deal would narrow the cushion further; we rate the risk moderate until terms are known.
risks.systemic:
ADI's results follow the broad semiconductor and industrial cycle. The 10-Q lists "changes in demand for semiconductor products" and "economic, political, legal and regulatory uncertainty or conflicts" among the factors that could change results, and the fiscal 2025 10-K adds inflation, tariffs and trade restrictions, high interest rates and "slower economic growth or recession."

Trade policy is a live variable. The 10-K notes that in April 2025 the Department of Commerce launched a Section 232 investigation into imported semiconductors and semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and that the global trade situation "continues to be highly dynamic." It also cites tensions across the Taiwan Strait, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, and tensions in Israel and the Middle East.

The data center demand behind this year's Communications growth also depends on one spending theme: a pause in artificial intelligence-related infrastructure investment would hit Communications, which grew 84% year over year in the quarter. These risks are shared across the sector; ADI's breadth spreads them but does not remove them.

body: We rate Analog Devices HOLD with a target range of $430–$470. ADI is a strong franchise executing well, and the problem is the entry price at this point in the cycle, not the business. The price assumes fiscal 2027 goes right, and our weighting of the alternatives leaves too little expected return for the cyclical risk that comes with it.

We would move to BUY if the fourth-quarter results and the next outlook point to fiscal 2027 EPS above the FY27E consensus of $16.35 with adjusted operating margin holding near the approximately 52.0% guided for the fourth quarter, or if the shares fell toward the bottom of the Street target range with consensus intact. We would move to SELL if fourth-quarter revenue fell below the bottom of the outlook range, or the next quarterly outlook pointed below the FY27E consensus path, while the shares stayed near their high; or if the shares rose well above our target range without higher estimates.
